title: PWM: Faking In-Between Values
description: A digital pin can't output half-voltage — so how does ARIA dim an LED, or set a motor to half speed? By blinking, very fast, and lying to your eyes about it.

content.value: Last lesson's rule was strict: a digital pin is only ever HIGH or LOW. But plenty of things a robot needs aren't binary — a dimmer LED, a motor running at half speed, a servo holding a precise in-between angle. If the pin genuinely can't do "half on", how does any of that work?
The Trick: Blink Faster Than You Can See

The pin still only ever outputs HIGH or LOW — but it switches between them so fast, dozens or hundreds of times a second, that your eye can't follow the individual flips. What you perceive instead is an average: an LED that's on 75% of the time and off 25% looks like a dimmer, steady LED, even though at any single instant it's actually fully on or fully off.
This trick is called PWM — Pulse Width Modulation. "Pulse width" is exactly what it sounds like: how wide (how long) each HIGH pulse is, out of one full cycle.

content.title: 🔆 Drag the duty cycle, then slow the frequency
content.hint: Set duty to about 50%, then drag frequency all the way down. The steady dimming will resolve into visible blinking — that's the illusion breaking.

content.value: The percentage of each cycle spent HIGH is called the duty cycle. 100% duty is indistinguishable from just leaving the pin on. 0% duty is the same as leaving it off. Everything useful happens in between.

25% duty   ▔▁▁▁ ▔▁▁▁ ▔▁▁▁     dim LED, slow motor
50% duty   ▔▔▁▁ ▔▔▁▁ ▔▔▁▁     half-bright LED, half-speed motor
90% duty   ▔▔▔▁ ▔▔▔▁ ▔▔▔▁     nearly full brightness/speed

Frequency is how many of those cycles happen per second, measured in Hz. It needs to be fast enough that you (or a motor's own mechanical sluggishness) can't follow the individual flips — typically somewhere from a few hundred to a few thousand Hz on real hardware, though the widget above deliberately lets you go slow enough to see the trick break.

A motor doesn't have eyes to fool — but it does have physical inertia, which averages out fast on/off pulses into smooth partial-speed spinning the same way your eye averages out an LED's flicker into a dimmer glow. Same trick, different reason it works.

Key takeaway: PWM fakes an in-between value by rapidly switching a digital pin HIGH and LOW. Duty cycle (percent of time HIGH) controls the apparent brightness or speed; frequency just needs to be fast enough that the flicker isn't perceptible.

quiz.question: Is a PWM pin ever actually outputting a half-voltage signal?
options: Yes, PWM genuinely outputs in-between voltages
No — it's always fully HIGH or fully LOW, just switching fast enough that it looks in-between
Only on Arduino boards, not ESP32
quiz.explain: PWM never leaves the digital HIGH/LOW world. It fakes an average by controlling how much time is spent in each state.

quiz.question: An LED is driven with a 20% duty cycle. Roughly how does it look?
options: Dim — noticeably darker than full brightness, but not off
quiz.explain: 20% duty means the pin is HIGH only a fifth of the time. Averaged by your eye, that reads as a dim glow rather than full brightness or darkness.

quiz.question: In the widget, dragging frequency down to about 1–2 Hz breaks the illusion. Why?
options: Low frequency actually changes the duty cycle
The individual on/off flips become slow enough for your eye to follow them directly, instead of averaging them
It doesn't break anything, that's a bug
quiz.explain: PWM relies on flips being too fast to perceive. Slow them down enough and you're just watching a blinking light, one flip at a time.

quiz.question: Why does duty cycle work for controlling a DC motor's speed, even though the motor never actually gets a fractional voltage either?
options: Motors have physical inertia that smooths rapid on/off pulses into an averaged, slower spin — the same averaging trick, for a mechanical reason instead of a visual one
Motors secretly can read in-between voltages
It doesn't work for motors, only LEDs
quiz.explain: The motor's own mechanical sluggishness plays the same role your eye plays for an LED — it can't react to each individual pulse, so it responds to the average.
